claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple single-phase solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
This alloy state has favorable plasticity or ductility and machinability.
The low hardness and strength arise from insufficient lattice distortion.
The low hardness and strength arise from a lack of nanoscale obstacles to dislocation motion.
The simple solid solution provides only minimal solid-solution strengthening.
Minimal solid-solution strengthening permits extensive dislocation glide.
Grain-boundary-mediated plasticity contributes to the favorable plasticity and machinability.
Grain-boundary sliding occurs in the as-cast simple solid solution under the proposed loading conditions.
Controlled thermal aging can nucleate nanoscale ordered domains or fine precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
The aging-induced ordered domains or precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Aging-induced ordering or precipitation increases lattice friction.
Aging-induced ordering or precipitation pins dislocations.
Thermal aging should increase both hardness and yield strength by more than 10% relative to the as-quenched state.
TEM or XRD should reveal nanoscale obstacles in aged samples that are absent from unaged samples.
The comparison should hold composition and grain-size distribution approximately constant while varying thermal aging.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under quasi-static loading from room temperature to about 700°C.
The kinetics of nanoscale ordering or precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi are not well established.
The quantitative effect of ordering or precipitation on dislocation mobility is not well established.

contradictions.description: The boundary describes applicability to material having a similar single-phase solid-solution microstructure, whereas the intervention and predicted outcome require formation of precipitates or ordered domains, which may make the aged comparison structurally multiphase or otherwise no longer the same simple single-phase state.
